analysis.one_liner: Freezes major federal regulations until unemployment falls to 7.7 percent or below.
analysis.headline: The bill never advanced past committee referral and died without a House vote when the 112th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have barred every federal agency from taking any 'significant regulatory action' — a definition so broad it covers most major rules, including ones affecting the economy, environment, public health, safety, and small businesses — until quarterly average unemployment dropped to 7.7% or lower. The President could waive the freeze only for national security or national emergencies, or by asking Congress. Businesses could sue over rules issued in violation and collect attorney fees if they won.
analysis.who_benefits: Businesses that would have been subject to major new federal rules — on pollution, workplace safety, consumer protection, financial practices, and more — would gain a potentially years-long freeze on those rules. Any regulated party could also sue to block a rule issued in violation of the freeze and recover attorney fees, and small businesses would get fee awards even when an agency merely changed course after being sued.

how_it_helps.text: Bars agencies from taking any significant regulatory action until the BLS quarterly average unemployment rate is 7.7% or lower [S2][S3].

Defines 'significant' broadly to include rules with a $100 million annual economic effect or that materially affect the economy, jobs, the environment, public health or safety, or small entities — covering most major federal rules [S2][S3].
Gives any adversely affected person court access to block or strike down rules issued in violation, with attorney fees awarded to substantially prevailing small businesses [S3].
Allows the President to waive the freeze for national security or national emergencies, and to request congressional waivers for other rules [S2][S3].

analysis.who_pays: Ordinary people would bear the cost of delayed protections: clean air and water rules, workplace and product safety standards, consumer and financial safeguards, and public health measures would all sit frozen while unemployment stayed above the trigger. Workers, consumers, and communities exposed to unaddressed hazards would wait, while the businesses the rules targeted kept operating under the older, weaker rules.

drawbacks.text: The freeze would not distinguish helpful rules from costly ones: it blocks every significant rule, including those protecting public health, safety, and the environment, for as long as unemployment stayed above 7.7% [S2][S3].
A regulation freeze does not itself create jobs, and delaying protections could shift costs onto the public — for example, in health harms or cleanup expenses — rather than eliminating them [S3].

Supporters' honest case: businesses argue regulatory uncertainty and compliance costs deter hiring during high unemployment, so a pause would remove a barrier to job creation — the bill's own premise, reflected in its title [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill would hand regulated businesses a blanket multi-year pause on most major federal rules, with no weighing of whether each rule's benefits exceed its costs. Whatever relief it offered employers on compliance costs would come at the price of delaying health, safety, environmental, and financial protections for everyone else, with no guarantee of job gains in return.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and referred to two House committees, then to subcommittees, and never received a markup or a floor vote before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Reid Ribble introduced the bill on September 12, 2011, and it was referred to the House Oversight and Government Reform and Judiciary Committees [S5].
In late September and early October 2011 it was referred to subcommittees of those committees, and no further action — no markup, no committee vote, no floor vote — is recorded [S5].
Seventy-seven Republicans cosponsored the bill, all from the party holding the House majority, yet the House never voted on it [S4].
The Congress ended January 3, 2013, so the bill died without ever coming to a vote [S1].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: People who rely on federal health, safety, environmental, and financial protections — the rules the bill would have frozen were free to move forward. Businesses facing pending major rules gained nothing from the bill's death; they remain subject to the normal rulemaking process.

for.name: Rep. Reid Ribble
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill proposing a moratorium on significant regulatory actions until unemployment fell to 7.7% or below.

for.name: 77 House Republicans
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill after its introduction.

sides.party_line_note: The sponsor and all 77 cosponsors were Republicans, with no Democratic cosponsors listed; the bill then stalled in committee without a vote.

industries.industry: Businesses facing major federal rules (pollution, workplace safety, consumer and financial regulation)
industries.note: The bill would freeze nearly all significant federal rulemaking — including rules affecting the environment, public health and safety, and the economy — until unemployment hit 7.7%, letting regulated firms operate under older, weaker rules for years. The savings to firms would come from rules ordinary people never got: cleaner air and water, safer workplaces and products, and stronger financial safeguards [S2][S3].

The bill defines 'small entity' broadly and would let small businesses sue over rulemaking done in violation of the freeze, with attorney fees awarded even when an agency merely changes position after a suit. This reduces legal costs for small firms, but the freeze itself would also delay rules that benefit small businesses and their workers as consumers and employees [S3].
